definition: Articulatory speech recognition means the recovery of speech (in forms of phonemes, syllables or words) from acoustic signals with the help of articulatory modeling or an extra input of articulatory movement data.
details: Speech recognition (or automatic speech recognition, acoustic speech recognition) means the recovery of speech from acoustics (sound wave) only. Articulatory information is extremely helpful when the acoustic input is in low quality, perhaps because of noise or missing data. Measurable information from the articulatory system (e.g. tongue, jaw movements) can supplement acoustic signals to improve phone recognition accuracy by 2%. However, attempts to estimate articulatory data from acoustic signals alone have not significantly enhanced recognition performance.

explainer.lead: Articulatory speech recognition helps a computer work out what was said by using more than sound alone. It combines audio with knowledge or measurements of how speech organs such as the tongue and jaw move, which is especially useful when a recording is noisy or incomplete.

tiers.eli5: It is like trying to understand a friend over a crackly phone while also getting clues about how their mouth is moving. The computer listens to the sound and may also use measurements of the tongue or jaw. Those extra clues can help it work out the sounds, syllables, or words.
tiers.practitioner: This approach augments acoustic recognition with an articulatory model or an additional stream of measured articulatory movement, such as tongue or jaw motion. It is most useful for noisy audio or missing acoustic data, and measured articulatory information can improve phone recognition accuracy by 2%. A key pitfall is expecting the same benefit from articulatory data estimated from audio alone, which has not significantly improved recognition performance.
tiers.paperLevel: Let A be the acoustic signal and M optional articulatory movement data; the task is to recover a phoneme, syllable, or word sequence Y using an articulatory model or a mapping based on both A and M, rather than acoustics alone. Supplementing A with measurable articulatory information can improve phone recognition accuracy by 2%, particularly when A is noisy or incomplete. Estimating M from A alone has not significantly enhanced recognition performance.

explainer.example: Suppose background noise obscures part of a spoken word. A recognizer can combine the damaged audio with measured tongue and jaw movements to help choose the phoneme sequence and recover the word; such articulatory measurements can improve phone recognition accuracy by 2%.

explainer.intuition: Speech is produced by moving parts of the body, so those movements carry clues about what was said. Adding them to the sound gives the recognizer another source of evidence when listening alone is not enough.
howItWorks: Add an articulatory model or measured movement data, such as tongue or jaw motion.
Use the articulatory information to supplement the acoustic evidence.
Recover the corresponding phonemes, syllables, or words.
explainer.whyItMatters: Ordinary speech recognition depends entirely on sound, so noise or missing audio can remove crucial evidence. Articulatory information offers a separate clue about the speech being produced and can improve recognition in those difficult conditions.
misconceptions: It is not simply another name for ordinary automatic speech recognition, which uses acoustics alone.
Estimating articulatory movements from audio has not brought the significant gains seen with measured articulatory information.
